법적 고지

유료 서비스 이용약관

SC4SAP 유료 요금제의 결제, 갱신, 해지와 환불에 적용되는 약관입니다.

  • 시행일출시 시 확정
  • 버전2026-10-20.2
  • 판매자에스에이치랩솔루션즈

초안입니다. 본 약관은 아직 법률 자문의 검토를 거치지 않았고, 결제 연동도 아직 시작되지 않았습니다. 통신판매업 신고번호가 확정되고 시행일이 실제 날짜로 정해지기 전까지 이 페이지의 어떠한 내용도 귀하와 회사를 구속하지 않습니다.

결제하기 전에 제5조(요금)와 제9조(청약철회와 환불)를 읽으시기 바랍니다. 이 약관에서 정하지 않은 사항은 서비스 이용약관과 개인정보 처리방침, 그리고 「전자상거래 등에서의 소비자보호에 관한 법률」 등 관계 법령을 따릅니다.

목차
  1. 1.목적
  2. 2.용어의 정의
  3. 3.약관의 게시와 변경
  4. 4.유료 서비스의 내용
  5. 5.요금제와 요금
  6. 6.이용계약의 성립과 결제
  7. 7.자동 갱신과 결제 실패
  8. 8.해지
  9. 9.청약철회와 환불
  10. 10.AI 처리
  11. 11.서비스의 변경과 종료
  12. 12.분쟁 해결
  13. 13.판매자 정보와 언어

1.목적

이 약관은 에스에이치랩솔루션즈(이하 “회사”)가 제공하는 SC4SAP(이하 “서비스”)의 유료 요금제(이하 “유료 서비스”)에 관하여, 회사와 유료 서비스를 이용하는 회원 사이의 계약 체결, 결제, 갱신, 해지, 환불 및 그 밖에 필요한 사항을 정하는 것을 목적으로 합니다.

2.용어의 정의

  1. “회원”이란 서비스 이용약관에 동의하고 계정을 만든 자를 말합니다.
  2. “유료 회원”이란 유료 서비스 이용계약을 체결한 회원을 말합니다.
  3. “사용량 포함 요금제”란 회사의 Anthropic 계정으로 AI 처리가 이루어지고, 매월 정해진 한도(이하 “포함 사용량”)까지의 사용료가 요금에 포함된 요금제를 말합니다.
  4. “크레딧”이란 사용량 포함 요금제의 포함 사용량을 넘어 이용하기 위하여 회원이 유상으로 충전하는 사용량을 말합니다. 크레딧은 화폐가 아니며 양도할 수 없습니다.
  5. “결제대행사”란 회사를 대신해 결제를 처리하는 전자지급결제대행업자(토스페이먼츠 주식회사 등)를 말합니다.

3.약관의 게시와 변경

  1. 회사는 이 약관을 회원이 쉽게 볼 수 있도록 서비스 화면에 게시합니다.
  2. 회사는 관계 법령을 위반하지 않는 범위에서 이 약관을 변경할 수 있습니다. 변경 시 적용일과 변경 사유를 명시하여 적용일 7일 전부터 공지하며, 요금·결제·해지·환불 등 회원에게 불리한 변경은 적용일 30일 전부터 공지하고 이메일로 개별 통지합니다.
  3. 회원은 변경에 동의하지 않을 경우 적용일 전에 유료 서비스를 해지할 수 있습니다. 회사가 공지하면서 이를 함께 알렸음에도 회원이 적용일까지 거부 의사를 표시하지 않으면 변경에 동의한 것으로 봅니다. 다만 요금 인상에는 이 항을 적용하지 않고 제5조 제4항을 따릅니다.

4.유료 서비스의 내용

  1. 유료 서비스는 서비스의 모든 Skill과 문서 생성 기능, 계정별 여러 SAP 시스템 연결, 다국어 화면을 제공합니다.
  2. AI가 만든 결과물은 자격 있는 사람이 검토할 초안이며, 회사는 그 정확성이나 특정 목적 적합성을 보증하지 않습니다. 결과물을 SAP 시스템에 반영할지는 회원이 결정합니다(서비스 이용약관 제9조, 제10조).
  3. 회사는 운영상·기술상 필요에 따라 유료 서비스의 세부 기능을 개선하거나 변경할 수 있습니다. 주요 기능을 없애거나 회원에게 불리하게 바꾸는 경우 제11조를 따릅니다.

5.요금제와 요금

유료 서비스의 요금은 다음과 같으며, 모든 금액은 부가가치세를 포함합니다.

요금제월간 결제연간 결제포함 사용량
사용량 포함₩ 79,000 / 월₩ 790,000 / 년매월 미화 35달러 상당
  1. 크레딧은 ₩ 10,000에 미화 5달러 상당 사용량 단위로 충전합니다.
  2. 사용량은 Anthropic이 공시한 모델별 표준 단가로 계산하며, 회원은 설정 화면에서 언제든 남은 사용량을 확인할 수 있습니다.
  3. 신규 회원에게는 처음 Session을 시작한 날부터 7일 동안 미화 3달러 상당까지 무료 체험을 제공합니다. 무료 체험은 유료 요금제로 자동 전환되지 않으며, 체험이 끝나면 회원이 요금제를 선택해 결제해야 계속 이용할 수 있습니다.
  4. 회사는 요금을 변경할 수 있습니다. 요금을 올리는 경우 회사는 적용일 30일 전까지 인상 전후 금액, 적용일, 동의 방법과 해지 방법을 이메일로 개별 통지하고, 인상된 요금으로 처음 결제하기 전에 회원의 동의를 받습니다. 회원이 동의하지 않으면 인상된 요금으로 갱신하거나 결제하지 않으며, 유료 서비스는 이미 결제한 기간이 끝날 때 종료됩니다. 요금을 내리는 경우에는 다음 갱신일부터 내린 요금을 적용합니다.

6.이용계약의 성립과 결제

  1. 유료 서비스 이용계약은 회원이 결제 화면에서 요금제, 결제 주기, 금액, 자동 갱신 여부와 이 약관을 확인하고 동의한 뒤 결제가 승인되었을 때 성립합니다.
  2. 회사는 「전자상거래법」 제7조에 따라, 결제하기 전에 결제 금액, 결제 주기, 자동 갱신 여부를 회원이 확인하고 정정하거나 취소할 수 있는 확인 단계를 제공합니다.
  3. 결제는 결제대행사를 통해 신용카드·체크카드 등 결제대행사가 제공하는 수단으로 합니다. 카드 번호 등 결제수단 정보는 결제대행사가 보관하며 회사는 이를 저장하지 않습니다.
  4. 미성년자가 유료 서비스를 이용하려면 법정대리인의 동의가 필요하며, 법정대리인의 동의 없이 체결된 계약은 미성년자 본인 또는 법정대리인이 취소할 수 있습니다.
  5. 회사는 결제가 완료되면 결제 내역을 회원의 이메일로 보냅니다.

7.자동 갱신과 결제 실패

  1. 유료 서비스는 회원이 해지하기 전까지 같은 요금제와 결제 주기로 자동 갱신되며, 갱신일에 등록된 결제수단으로 요금이 자동 결제됩니다.
  2. 연간 결제 회원에게는 갱신일 7일 전까지 갱신 예정 사실과 금액을 이메일로 알립니다.
  3. 갱신 결제가 실패하면 회사는 회원에게 알리고 3일 동안 결제를 다시 시도합니다. 그래도 결제되지 않으면 유료 서비스 이용이 정지되며, 회원이 결제수단을 갱신해 결제하면 다시 이용할 수 있습니다.

8.해지

  1. 회원은 설정 화면에서 언제든 유료 서비스를 해지할 수 있습니다.
  2. 해지하면 다음 갱신 결제가 이루어지지 않으며, 이미 결제한 기간이 끝날 때까지는 유료 서비스를 계속 이용할 수 있습니다. 환불은 제9조를 따릅니다.
  3. 회원이 서비스 이용약관을 중대하게 위반한 경우 회사는 사전 통지 후 이용계약을 해지할 수 있으며, 이 경우 남은 기간의 요금은 제9조 제4항의 방식으로 계산해 환불합니다.

9.청약철회와 환불

  1. 회원은 결제일로부터 7일 이내에 청약을 철회할 수 있으며, 그 기간 동안 유료 기능(Session 실행, 문서 생성 등)을 한 번도 이용하지 않았다면 결제 금액 전액을 환불받습니다.
  2. 유료 서비스는 이용을 시작하면 그 가치가 제공되는 디지털 콘텐츠이므로, 유료 기능을 이용한 뒤에는 「전자상거래법」 제17조 제2항 제5호에 따라 청약철회가 제한됩니다. 회사는 결제 화면에서 이 사실을 미리 알립니다.
  3. 제2항에도 불구하고 연간 결제 회원이 결제일로부터 7일 이내에 청약을 철회하는 경우, 회사는 이미 이용을 시작한 달의 요금(연간 결제 요금의 12분의 1)만 빼고 나머지를 환불합니다. 아직 시작되지 않은 달은 제공이 개시되지 않은 부분으로 봅니다.
  4. 연간 결제 회원이 결제일로부터 7일이 지난 뒤 해지하는 경우, 회사는 결제 금액에서 이용한 개월 수(시작한 달은 한 달로 셉니다)에 월간 결제 요금을 곱한 금액을 뺀 나머지를 환불합니다.
  5. 회사의 귀책사유로 유료 서비스를 이용하지 못한 경우, 이용하지 못한 기간에 해당하는 요금을 환불하거나 같은 기간만큼 이용 기간을 연장합니다.
  6. 충전한 크레딧은 충전일로부터 7일 이내이고 사용하지 않았다면 전액을, 그 이후에는 남은 크레딧 금액의 90%를 환불합니다. 사용량 포함 요금제의 포함 사용량은 그 달에만 쓸 수 있으며 다음 달로 이월되거나 환불되지 않습니다.
  7. 회사는 환불 요청을 받은 날(청약철회의 경우 재화 등을 반환받은 날에 해당하는 날)로부터 3영업일 이내에 결제한 수단으로 환불합니다. 카드 결제 취소가 반영되는 시점은 카드사에 따라 다를 수 있습니다.
  8. 회원 본인의 과실로 제3자가 결제한 경우에도 환불은 이 조의 기준을 따릅니다. 다만 도용 등 법령이 정한 사유가 있으면 그에 따릅니다.

10.AI 처리

  1. 서비스의 AI 처리는 모두 회사의 Anthropic 계정으로 이루어집니다. 회원은 API 키를 등록하지 않습니다.
  2. AI 사용료는 제5조에 따라 포함 사용량과 크레딧에서 차감합니다. 회원은 Anthropic에 별도의 사용료를 내지 않습니다.

1.목적

이 약관은 에스에이치랩솔루션즈(이하 “회사”)가 제공하는 SC4SAP(이하 “서비스”)의 유료 요금제(이하 “유료 서비스”)에 관하여, 회사와 유료 서비스를 이용하는 회원 사이의 계약 체결, 결제, 갱신, 해지, 환불 및 그 밖에 필요한 사항을 정하는 것을 목적으로 합니다.

2.용어의 정의

  1. “회원”이란 서비스 이용약관에 동의하고 계정을 만든 자를 말합니다.
  2. “유료 회원”이란 유료 서비스 이용계약을 체결한 회원을 말합니다.
  3. “사용량 포함 요금제”란 회사의 Anthropic 계정으로 AI 처리가 이루어지고, 매월 정해진 한도(이하 “포함 사용량”)까지의 사용료가 요금에 포함된 요금제를 말합니다.
  4. “크레딧”이란 사용량 포함 요금제의 포함 사용량을 넘어 이용하기 위하여 회원이 유상으로 충전하는 사용량을 말합니다. 크레딧은 화폐가 아니며 양도할 수 없습니다.
  5. “결제대행사”란 회사를 대신해 결제를 처리하는 전자지급결제대행업자(토스페이먼츠 주식회사 등)를 말합니다.

3.약관의 게시와 변경

  1. 회사는 이 약관을 회원이 쉽게 볼 수 있도록 서비스 화면에 게시합니다.
  2. 회사는 관계 법령을 위반하지 않는 범위에서 이 약관을 변경할 수 있습니다. 변경 시 적용일과 변경 사유를 명시하여 적용일 7일 전부터 공지하며, 요금·결제·해지·환불 등 회원에게 불리한 변경은 적용일 30일 전부터 공지하고 이메일로 개별 통지합니다.
  3. 회원은 변경에 동의하지 않을 경우 적용일 전에 유료 서비스를 해지할 수 있습니다. 회사가 공지하면서 이를 함께 알렸음에도 회원이 적용일까지 거부 의사를 표시하지 않으면 변경에 동의한 것으로 봅니다. 다만 요금 인상에는 이 항을 적용하지 않고 제5조 제4항을 따릅니다.

4.유료 서비스의 내용

  1. 유료 서비스는 서비스의 모든 Skill과 문서 생성 기능, 계정별 여러 SAP 시스템 연결, 다국어 화면을 제공합니다.
  2. AI가 만든 결과물은 자격 있는 사람이 검토할 초안이며, 회사는 그 정확성이나 특정 목적 적합성을 보증하지 않습니다. 결과물을 SAP 시스템에 반영할지는 회원이 결정합니다(서비스 이용약관 제9조, 제10조).
  3. 회사는 운영상·기술상 필요에 따라 유료 서비스의 세부 기능을 개선하거나 변경할 수 있습니다. 주요 기능을 없애거나 회원에게 불리하게 바꾸는 경우 제11조를 따릅니다.

5.요금제와 요금

유료 서비스의 요금은 다음과 같으며, 모든 금액은 부가가치세를 포함합니다.

요금제월간 결제연간 결제포함 사용량
사용량 포함₩ 79,000 / 월₩ 790,000 / 년매월 미화 35달러 상당
  1. 크레딧은 ₩ 10,000에 미화 5달러 상당 사용량 단위로 충전합니다.
  2. 사용량은 Anthropic이 공시한 모델별 표준 단가로 계산하며, 회원은 설정 화면에서 언제든 남은 사용량을 확인할 수 있습니다.
  3. 신규 회원에게는 처음 Session을 시작한 날부터 7일 동안 미화 3달러 상당까지 무료 체험을 제공합니다. 무료 체험은 유료 요금제로 자동 전환되지 않으며, 체험이 끝나면 회원이 요금제를 선택해 결제해야 계속 이용할 수 있습니다.
  4. 회사는 요금을 변경할 수 있습니다. 요금을 올리는 경우 회사는 적용일 30일 전까지 인상 전후 금액, 적용일, 동의 방법과 해지 방법을 이메일로 개별 통지하고, 인상된 요금으로 처음 결제하기 전에 회원의 동의를 받습니다. 회원이 동의하지 않으면 인상된 요금으로 갱신하거나 결제하지 않으며, 유료 서비스는 이미 결제한 기간이 끝날 때 종료됩니다. 요금을 내리는 경우에는 다음 갱신일부터 내린 요금을 적용합니다.

6.이용계약의 성립과 결제

  1. 유료 서비스 이용계약은 회원이 결제 화면에서 요금제, 결제 주기, 금액, 자동 갱신 여부와 이 약관을 확인하고 동의한 뒤 결제가 승인되었을 때 성립합니다.
  2. 회사는 「전자상거래법」 제7조에 따라, 결제하기 전에 결제 금액, 결제 주기, 자동 갱신 여부를 회원이 확인하고 정정하거나 취소할 수 있는 확인 단계를 제공합니다.
  3. 결제는 결제대행사를 통해 신용카드·체크카드 등 결제대행사가 제공하는 수단으로 합니다. 카드 번호 등 결제수단 정보는 결제대행사가 보관하며 회사는 이를 저장하지 않습니다.
  4. 미성년자가 유료 서비스를 이용하려면 법정대리인의 동의가 필요하며, 법정대리인의 동의 없이 체결된 계약은 미성년자 본인 또는 법정대리인이 취소할 수 있습니다.
  5. 회사는 결제가 완료되면 결제 내역을 회원의 이메일로 보냅니다.

7.자동 갱신과 결제 실패

  1. 유료 서비스는 회원이 해지하기 전까지 같은 요금제와 결제 주기로 자동 갱신되며, 갱신일에 등록된 결제수단으로 요금이 자동 결제됩니다.
  2. 연간 결제 회원에게는 갱신일 7일 전까지 갱신 예정 사실과 금액을 이메일로 알립니다.
  3. 갱신 결제가 실패하면 회사는 회원에게 알리고 3일 동안 결제를 다시 시도합니다. 그래도 결제되지 않으면 유료 서비스 이용이 정지되며, 회원이 결제수단을 갱신해 결제하면 다시 이용할 수 있습니다.

8.해지

  1. 회원은 설정 화면에서 언제든 유료 서비스를 해지할 수 있습니다.
  2. 해지하면 다음 갱신 결제가 이루어지지 않으며, 이미 결제한 기간이 끝날 때까지는 유료 서비스를 계속 이용할 수 있습니다. 환불은 제9조를 따릅니다.
  3. 회원이 서비스 이용약관을 중대하게 위반한 경우 회사는 사전 통지 후 이용계약을 해지할 수 있으며, 이 경우 남은 기간의 요금은 제9조 제4항의 방식으로 계산해 환불합니다.

9.청약철회와 환불

  1. 회원은 결제일로부터 7일 이내에 청약을 철회할 수 있으며, 그 기간 동안 유료 기능(Session 실행, 문서 생성 등)을 한 번도 이용하지 않았다면 결제 금액 전액을 환불받습니다.
  2. 유료 서비스는 이용을 시작하면 그 가치가 제공되는 디지털 콘텐츠이므로, 유료 기능을 이용한 뒤에는 「전자상거래법」 제17조 제2항 제5호에 따라 청약철회가 제한됩니다. 회사는 결제 화면에서 이 사실을 미리 알립니다.
  3. 제2항에도 불구하고 연간 결제 회원이 결제일로부터 7일 이내에 청약을 철회하는 경우, 회사는 이미 이용을 시작한 달의 요금(연간 결제 요금의 12분의 1)만 빼고 나머지를 환불합니다. 아직 시작되지 않은 달은 제공이 개시되지 않은 부분으로 봅니다.
  4. 연간 결제 회원이 결제일로부터 7일이 지난 뒤 해지하는 경우, 회사는 결제 금액에서 이용한 개월 수(시작한 달은 한 달로 셉니다)에 월간 결제 요금을 곱한 금액을 뺀 나머지를 환불합니다.
  5. 회사의 귀책사유로 유료 서비스를 이용하지 못한 경우, 이용하지 못한 기간에 해당하는 요금을 환불하거나 같은 기간만큼 이용 기간을 연장합니다.
  6. 충전한 크레딧은 충전일로부터 7일 이내이고 사용하지 않았다면 전액을, 그 이후에는 남은 크레딧 금액의 90%를 환불합니다. 사용량 포함 요금제의 포함 사용량은 그 달에만 쓸 수 있으며 다음 달로 이월되거나 환불되지 않습니다.
  7. 회사는 환불 요청을 받은 날(청약철회의 경우 재화 등을 반환받은 날에 해당하는 날)로부터 3영업일 이내에 결제한 수단으로 환불합니다. 카드 결제 취소가 반영되는 시점은 카드사에 따라 다를 수 있습니다.
  8. 회원 본인의 과실로 제3자가 결제한 경우에도 환불은 이 조의 기준을 따릅니다. 다만 도용 등 법령이 정한 사유가 있으면 그에 따릅니다.

10.AI 처리

  1. 서비스의 AI 처리는 모두 회사의 Anthropic 계정으로 이루어집니다. 회원은 API 키를 등록하지 않습니다.
  2. AI 사용료는 제5조에 따라 포함 사용량과 크레딧에서 차감합니다. 회원은 Anthropic에 별도의 사용료를 내지 않습니다.

11.서비스의 변경과 종료

  1. 회사가 유료 서비스의 주요 기능을 없애거나 서비스를 종료하려는 경우, 그 30일 전까지 서비스 화면에 공지하고 유료 회원에게 이메일로 개별 통지합니다.
  2. 서비스 종료로 남은 기간을 이용할 수 없게 된 경우, 회사는 남은 기간의 요금과 남은 크레딧을 전액 환불합니다.

12.분쟁 해결

  1. 회사는 유료 서비스에 관한 회원의 의견과 불만을 처리하는 창구(sc4sap.dev@gmail.com, 010-8257-5798)를 운영하며, 접수한 사항은 지체 없이 처리 결과를 알립니다.
  2. 회원은 공정거래위원회 또는 시·도지사가 의뢰하는 분쟁조정기관(한국소비자원 등)에 피해구제나 분쟁조정을 신청할 수 있습니다.
  3. 이 약관과 유료 서비스에 관한 소송은 「민사소송법」에 따른 관할 법원에 제기합니다. 회원이 소비자인 경우 회원의 주소지를 관할하는 법원도 관할 법원이 됩니다.

content.text:
CLI 표현이 어디서 왔는지 찾았어요. 소개 페이지에 hanta의 CLI 백엔드 내용은 없어요. Claude Code를 가리키는 "CLI"라는 말만 들어가 있어요. 그래도 설치 환경에 hanta가 섞인 곳이 하나 있어서 같이 정리했어요.

## 소개 페이지 (SC4SAP — ERP AX의 새로운 첫걸음)

"CLI"가 나오는 곳은 4군데예요.

| 파일 | 문구 |
|---|---|
| `index.html`, `index_n.html` | 아이콘 툴팁 "VS Code · CLI 플러그인" (스크린리더용 설명에도 같은 말) |
| `service/about.html` | "Claude Code CLI 플러그인", "터미널이나 VS Code의…", 버튼 "설치 가이드(CLI)" |
| `resources/guide.html` | 제목 "설치 가이드(CLI)", 요구사항 "Claude Code: CLI 설치 완료" |
| `resources/brochure.html` | 링크 "설치 가이드(CLI)" |

- **내용은 모두 MCP 방식이에요.** MCP 서버 자동 설치, `/mcp` 재연결, "MCP 서버 자체 가드"를 설명해요.
- **hanta 고유 내용은 없어요.** `sc4sap-cli`, `--allow-write`, 승인 창, 감사 로그(audit log) 같은 말이 한 번도 나오지 않아요.
- **출처는 공개 설치 문서예요.** `guide.html`의 주석에 옛 랜딩 사이트 install.html에서 가져왔다고 적혀 있어요. 그 원본은 `docs/INSTALLATION.ko.md`이고, 여기에 "Claude_Code-CLI" 배지와 "CLI 설치 완료" 문구가 있어요. 이 "CLI"는 Claude Code라는 프로그램을 가리켜요.
- **문제는 읽는 사람이 헷갈린다는 점이에요.** "CLI 플러그인"이나 "설치 가이드(CLI)"는 hanta의 CLI 연결 방식처럼 읽혀요.

## sc4sap · abap-mcp-adt-powerup 리포

- **README에는 CLI가 추가되지 않았어요.** `sc4sap/README*.md`에는 CLI라는 말이 없어요.
- **hanta 용어도 없어요.** `sc4sap-cli`, `bin/sc4sap-cli` 같은 말은 docs, skills, MCP 리포 어디에도 없어요.
- **MCP README의 "CLI Options"는 정상이에요.** MCP 서버를 실행할 때 쓰는 인자 설명이에요.
- **`sc4sap/package.json`에 잘못된 줄이 하나 있어요.** `"bin": {"sc4sap": "bridge/cli.cjs"}`가 v0.1.0 첫 커밋부터 남아 있어요. 그런데 이 파일은 없어요. hanta와는 무관하고, 정리하면 좋은 정도예요.

## 섞인 곳: 설치된 플러그인 캐시

- **공개판 캐시 폴더 안에 hanta 빌드가 있어요.** 위치는 `~/.claude/plugins/cache/sc4sap/sc4sap/0.6.53`이에요.
  - 홈페이지가 사내 GitLab(hq-git)이고, `bin/sc4sap-cli.cjs`가 들어 있어요.
  - `sc4sap-cli`를 언급하는 파일이 155개예요.
- **지금 실행 중인 버전은 공개판이에요.** 활성 플러그인은 `sc4sap@sc4sap` 0.6.55이고, 여기에는 hanta 내용이 없어요. `sc4sap@sc4sap-hanta`는 꺼져 있어요.
- **다만 위험이 남아 있어요.** 두 플러그인 이름이 둘 다 `sc4sap`이에요. 그래서 "sc4sap 캐시"를 폴더 이름으로 찾아 읽으면 hanta 내용이 공개판처럼 섞여 들어올 수 있어요. 그 폴더의 파일 날짜가 10-29이고, 소개 페이지를 마지막으로 고친 날도 10-29예요. 하지만 페이지에 hanta 고유 내용이 없으니, 실제로 거기서 가져왔을 가능성은 낮아 보여요.

## 제안 (아직 아무것도 고치지 않았어요)

1. **페이지 문구에서 CLI를 빼기:**

Back in the day, critical thinking was taught as approaching new info with humble curiosity and a healthy dose of skepticism - take in different views, form your own opinion. Still true, but increasingly, nothing in my day-to-day forces critical thinking on me now that so much of my work runs through agents. For the engineers and product people who have fully bought into agentic workflows (running multiple sessions in parallel and expecting the models to improve), I'm here to say: I'm a big fan of these tools. I'm not writing this to advocate for less agentic workflows.
My goal is to help you maintain critical thinking in a world where it's easy to offload anything to an agent.
In the past, most of our cognitive and aesthetic processing happened in the space between question and answer. That space is now measured in seconds. The more you use agentic workflows, the more difficult it becomes (though not in the way I think people expected): as the models improve, the percentage of obvious errors is lower. Many (most?) outputs will be well-written and mostly correct, but they won't demand a second look.
Even if you are running many agents at a time, you still only have one pair of eyes on the outputs.
You have to build critical thinking into your day, because by default nothing will do it for you.
Part of the reason it's hard to self-correct for this is that agentic workflows are pleasant. Getting fast, pleasant, often-correct answers is refreshing in a busy day, but that's also why it's easy to relax your vigilance.
Offloading, deferral and surrender
When discussing this with people, I describe it as a spectrum:
At the top: cognitive offloading, the act of delegating tasks to the AI, but maintaining ownership of the result. I do this all day. You should, too. In the middle: deferral, where the output of the tool becomes your new input; the result has ceased to be a hypothesis. At the bottom: cognitive surrender - the AI's output quietly becomes your own, you feel no need to check it.
Cognitive surrender is a term coined by Steven Shaw and Gideon Nave at Wharton. It fits neatly what I've been seeing: as trust (or laziness) increases, people drift down the spectrum. The transition is rarely observed, because the steps are each gradual and seem reasonable. You read the last answer well, so you skim the next one. You just scan the skeleton of the one after that. Then you get asked about a line and can't explain it, even with your agent's help.
That's cognitive surrender. It's how cognitive debt accumulates. It's usually discovered when you try to apply a mental model of the system and it doesn't exist. Margaret-Anne Storey has written about how this shows up in teams as an eroding understanding of a shared system theory. I've written about the code equivalent, comprehension debt (a term coined by Jeremy Twei). In the moment, it's completely invisible. The codebase looks pristine and the tests pass. It doesn't become obvious until you have to make a change to the system and realize that nobody understands it anymore. The same applies when you've read the table of contents of a strategy doc or spec and signed off on it.
To be clear, I'm not advocating for the impossible. It's impossible to maintain the full mental model of a large modern codebase. The Claude Code team has said publicly that they rebuild understanding on demand: when they need to understand a part, they ask Claude to explain that slice, rather than holding the full model in their heads. As I've written about before, this sort of debt is more recoverable than most engineers expect. You don't need to maintain the full model as long as you can rebuild it locally as needed. You just need to know what you don't have.
Where the stakes are low, feel free to delegate entirely. When you can't explain the answer to a question, even by way of your agent, you've ceded ownership. 
This isn't always a problem, either. Just recently, I was recording a course and had to select one out of three similarly-rated hotels to use as a recording location. I didn't have time to manually review all the reviews, so I delegated the decision to an AI. It worked, and I'd do the same thing again. However, I wouldn't do that when deciding how to invest our money, how to advise our kids on their careers, or at work: what we should build, what changes affect what users, whether it's safe to ship. Take the handoff where being wrong is cheap, keep the reasoning where others will have to deal with the consequences.
The questions I ask myself
When I didn't know what I thought, I'd usually go back to a basic list of questions like these: How do I know that I'm working on the right problem? How do I know that I'm solving it the right way? Is there evidence that supports my conclusion? How do I know that I'm finished? Most times, this is just who, what, where, why, when and how. When written out, it looks absurdly child-like, but it forces you to think in terms of categories that you'd otherwise ignore. These days, it's too easy to simply skip all of this and ask your agent what it thinks you should do. These are the new versions of these questions that I ask myself now.
Did I formulate a hypothesis before asking? Before I run an agent on any non-trivial task, I write down, even just in my head, what I think the answer might be. It's OK if it's a bad guess. You're always welcome to change your mind in light of new information. Once you've read a well-written response, though, it's hard to imagine any other possibility. If you have no guidance whatsoever, ask for what Thariq Shihipar calls a blind spot pass: give the model what you know and have it find your unknown unknowns.
Am I asking it to help me think or to offload thinking from me? Both are OK, as long as you know which one you're doing.
What would have to be true for this to be wrong? Then go find out. A model's self-assessment of confidence is much less valuable than an actual test you can perform, so give it one.
Have I heard the counter argument from a different angle? When I've taken a hard stance on something that's somewhat open-ended, I'll ask more than one model to argue the opposite side, then review the output and form my own opinion. This takes longer, but I end up knowing much more about the subject.
Would I bet on this in front of the person who has to maintain it? This applies to code and to anything else that you're delivering. I believe that this is the bar for answerability.
What am I no longer practicing? Maybe it's some of the routine debugging. I'm OK with letting some of that go, but I want it to be intentional.

I've been writing a lot about verification lately because I believe that the bottleneck has shifted from coding to being sure you're right. When you give an agent the means to verify what it's doing, whether that be by way of end-to-end tests, property tests, or by way of actual app interactions, it can make a change, run the verification test, read the output, and attempt again all before you've looked at anything. This is what Boris Cherny calls "give Claude a way to verify its work" and I believe that this is one of the most critical components of achieving great results. Rather than reading every line, you'll be building these loops and reviewing the evidence.
You can also surrender verification. "Is there evidence that supports my conclusion?" becomes "Did the check turn green?" Agents make it so cheap to create tests that you'll see a lot of green, and you could have a passing test that doesn't catch a broken feature. If the test is written with the same mistake as the feature, it'll pass. And a green check only conveys one property. It's too easy to imagine it covers everything.
When a check goes green, ask what it proved. Then ask what it didn't.

I still ask at the end "Did I miss anything?" That sounds silly, but so often, when I finish some complex feature work using a frontier model, look at it, review it, and then ask, "Did I miss anything?" It will then come back with two or three more things. That's why I always ask.
None of this needs to be the norm, of course; knowing when to go deep is a skill. My favorite rule of thumb from our write-up on how the Claude Code team does code review is: "If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval."
This applies beyond code as well. If an agent has synthesized fifty customer calls for you, or a competitive analysis, check a couple of the source documents to make sure the summary is accurate. Check a number that your recommendation depends on to make sure it's being calculated correctly.
Agents have made verification cheap to set up. What's difficult for you is knowing what good verification looks like.

Say an agent gives you a 600-line PR. You roughly look at the structure. You don't read every line. The variable names look reasonable and the tests pass, so you approve it. But somewhere in the middle there's a subtle ordering change in a transaction boundary, or a flipped default on an edge case you never thought about. You did review it, I guess, but only for what you already knew you'd find.
Writing code and reviewing it are different skills, and there's a point where reviewing turns into rubber stamping. So read the diff as if the AI didn't write it, and then look past the diff at what the agent decided. Over a long session it makes a lot of small decisions for you: the defaults, what's out of scope, which requirement it reinterprets when two of them clash.
You won't see any of that in a summary that says everything went well, so ask it to list the decisions and assumptions it made. Then quiz yourself. Pick a few lines at random and ask, what about this line? What about that one? For a document, close it and try to write out the main argument from memory. Some have a habit I like for long sessions: have Claude write a report on the change, and then give you a quiz at the bottom, where the rule is "I only merge after I pass the quiz perfectly."
Understand what you're shipping well enough to defend it. Because at some point, someone could ask.
Agents can also guard your attention. For example, I have an open source project that receives a lot of pull requests. I'll use agents to help determine what's incoming, what's contrary to our guidelines, and where my attention is likely required. I rarely let the agents self-determine this, but they can narrow it down to where I should focus my attention, and then I can actually think about whether these changes are solving the right problem in the right way.
Then there's volume, and you have to be honest with yourself about it. I've called this the orchestration tax. It's the gap between what your agents generate and what you'd feel comfortable putting your name on. If finished work is piling up faster than you can get through it, another session won't help until you've fixed that: tighten the checks so less of it needs you, or slow down.
When you're producing more than you can stand behind, you're no longer reviewing. You're hoping.
Quality in, quality out
The human mental model is still involved, but instead of in the middle, it's at the front and end. You're putting your energy into the front-end of the task description and context, as well as the back-end of reviewing the output. This is why good input is so important to the quality of output, and I view good prompting as a critical thinking skill.
Historically, if you made a non-specific request, someone would challenge it, and you might realize, "Oh wait, I actually didn't figure this out." An agent often won't stop you there. It fills in what you left out and hands back something that looks done, even though the idea behind it is still fuzzy. I've written about this as intent debt, the implicit goals, constraints and rationale that may exist in artifacts you didn't write. Unlike other kinds of debt, nobody else can fix this one for you. The intent has to come from you.
Your prompt is a reflection of your understanding of the problem, and if you can't express it clearly, it may not be clear in your own mind.
Write your own request brief in your own words before you ask for help. Describe the audience, out-of-scope items, and the definition of done. When your second round of corrections hasn't got you there, stop tweaking and rewrite your prompt.
You can have the agent help you with this too. I like the distinction Andy Clark makes between delegating to an AI system and collaborating with it. In the latter case, you're in a virtuous cycle of mutual amplification: your prompts sharpen your output, sharpen your next prompt and sharpen your mental model of the problem. If it's not clear, ask the agent to interview you about what it doesn't understand. If you close the session having refined your own mental model, that's a sign of success.
Also be careful about the input. It's easy for each agent to just pass the previous agent's summary into its context, and before long the third agent hasn't read the original document.
You also need your own standards for output. I've played around with AI in lots of different creative mediums, and most of it never gets shown because it doesn't meet my standards. Things are all coming out nicely formatted and confident, so polish is no longer a useful signal.
AI may have made it faster to produce, but if I wouldn't feel comfortable attributing the output to myself, I won't output it.
When something doesn't meet your standards, note why in shared config, a hook or a test so that it doesn't happen again. That's how taste compounds, and noting why something didn't make the cut is good practice on its own.
"But the models will be better at this than me"
If you're as bullish on the future of this space as many people around me are, you've probably had this thought for a couple of sections. In a year or two, the model will be able to detect what I'd be able to detect, so why bother maintaining the skill?
You may be right on a lot of that detection, and I've been arguing for increasingly pushing detection to agents myself. But here's why I think it still matters: at the end of the day, someone is responsible for what ships. Regardless of how much AI helped, a human has to take responsibility.
The question of how much to trust an agent for any given task is itself a judgment call. Part of staying calibrated is reviewing the work, because what the models get wrong keeps changing. Anthropic's own research on its engineers and researchers calls out the trap as the paradox of supervision: "supervising Claude requires the very coding skills that may atrophy from AI overuse."
These are some of the things that matter most to me and that a better model won't solve: what are you building, why is it worth it, who does it impact and what are you willing to sacrifice? Those are all questions you need to answer. An agent can be helpful in working them through, and I would like it to be, but ultimately they're still yours.
You may offload the work and much of the auditing, but not the accountability.
Practices for the everyday
You don't need to do all this rigorously. Just plug in what works for your workflow.
Once a week, write a bit of code without an agent, or do one real thing that would suck if you forgot how to do it. (I've called this a calibration exercise, but I don't mean it as a moral one.) Once a month, write down what you've stopped doing and decide which of those you're okay not doing. One question from an old blog post of mine remains as valid as ever: How lost would you be if AI didn't exist?
If something is above your comprehension, go learn it. If I'm writing and I run into a phrase I haven't seen before, I could Google a one-line explanation and include it. I prefer to do a little research to properly understand it, so I can see where it fits.
Checking the machine properly is real work, and pretending otherwise is how teams end up not doing it. It isn't free, so schedule it as a line item and you'll actually get it done.
Skills that you stop exercising are going to go away, and probably faster than you might guess. Keep doing the ones you're not willing to let go.
What to bring with you
Be intentional. An agent can quiz you, interview you and show you its evidence, but only if you set that up. So set it up.
Be honest about your place on the spectrum. If you can't explain the answer, even with an agent's help, you've surrendered it.
Have a hypothesis. Formulate one before asking, even if it's bad.
A green check means one thing. What did it check? What did it not check?
Look for evidence. Read what it ran and what it returned before reading the summary.
Read to know what decisions it made. What did it decide for you?
Craft your prompt. How you write what you prompt shows how much you understood the problem.
Set a bar, and stick to it. If you wouldn't put your name on it, it doesn't go out.
Keep yourself in the game by manually applying the skills that matter. One thing you could do: Before you ask, write down what you think will happen, and after the agent is done, write down one thing it didn't check. Let me know if that changes the way you read the output. Think independently. Ask better questions. Take responsibility for the outcome.

<pasted_content id="636e">
Back in the day, critical thinking was taught as approaching new info with humble curiosity and a healthy dose of skepticism - take in different views, form your own opinion. Still true, but increasingly, nothing in my day-to-day forces critical thinking on me now that so much of my work runs through agents. For the engineers and product people who have fully bought into agentic workflows (running multiple sessions in parallel and expecting the models to improve), I'm here to say: I'm a big fan of these tools. I'm not writing this to advocate for less agentic workflows.
My goal is to help you maintain critical thinking in a world where it's easy to offload anything to an agent.
In the past, most of our cognitive and aesthetic processing happened in the space between question and answer. That space is now measured in seconds. The more you use agentic workflows, the more difficult it becomes (though not in the way I think people expected): as the models improve, the percentage of obvious errors is lower. Many (most?) outputs will be well-written and mostly correct, but they won't demand a second look.
Even if you are running many agents at a time, you still only have one pair of eyes on the outputs.
You have to build critical thinking into your day, because by default nothing will do it for you.
Part of the reason it's hard to self-correct for this is that agentic workflows are pleasant. Getting fast, pleasant, often-correct answers is refreshing in a busy day, but that's also why it's easy to relax your vigilance.
Offloading, deferral and surrender
When discussing this with people, I describe it as a spectrum:
At the top: cognitive offloading, the act of delegating tasks to the AI, but maintaining ownership of the result. I do this all day. You should, too. In the middle: deferral, where the output of the tool becomes your new input; the result has ceased to be a hypothesis. At the bottom: cognitive surrender - the AI's output quietly becomes your own, you feel no need to check it.
Cognitive surrender is a term coined by Steven Shaw and Gideon Nave at Wharton. It fits neatly what I've been seeing: as trust (or laziness) increases, people drift down the spectrum. The transition is rarely observed, because the steps are each gradual and seem reasonable. You read the last answer well, so you skim the next one. You just scan the skeleton of the one after that. Then you get asked about a line and can't explain it, even with your agent's help.
That's cognitive surrender. It's how cognitive debt accumulates. It's usually discovered when you try to apply a mental model of the system and it doesn't exist. Margaret-Anne Storey has written about how this shows up in teams as an eroding understanding of a shared system theory. I've written about the code equivalent, comprehension debt (a term coined by Jeremy Twei). In the moment, it's completely invisible. The codebase looks pristine and the tests pass. It doesn't become obvious until you have to make a change to the system and realize that nobody understands it anymore. The same applies when you've read the table of contents of a strategy doc or spec and signed off on it.
To be clear, I'm not advocating for the impossible. It's impossible to maintain the full mental model of a large modern codebase. The Claude Code team has said publicly that they rebuild understanding on demand: when they need to understand a part, they ask Claude to explain that slice, rather than holding the full model in their heads. As I've written about before, this sort of debt is more recoverable than most engineers expect. You don't need to maintain the full model as long as you can rebuild it locally as needed. You just need to know what you don't have.
Where the stakes are low, feel free to delegate entirely. When you can't explain the answer to a question, even by way of your agent, you've ceded ownership. 
This isn't always a problem, either. Just recently, I was recording a course and had to select one out of three similarly-rated hotels to use as a recording location. I didn't have time to manually review all the reviews, so I delegated the decision to an AI. It worked, and I'd do the same thing again. However, I wouldn't do that when deciding how to invest our money, how to advise our kids on their careers, or at work: what we should build, what changes affect what users, whether it's safe to ship. Take the handoff where being wrong is cheap, keep the reasoning where others will have to deal with the consequences.
The questions I ask myself
When I didn't know what I thought, I'd usually go back to a basic list of questions like these: How do I know that I'm working on the right problem? How do I know that I'm solving it the right way? Is there evidence that supports my conclusion? How do I know that I'm finished? Most times, this is just who, what, where, why, when and how. When written out, it looks absurdly child-like, but it forces you to think in terms of categories that you'd otherwise ignore. These days, it's too easy to simply skip all of this and ask your agent what it thinks you should do. These are the new versions of these questions that I ask myself now.
Did I formulate a hypothesis before asking? Before I run an agent on any non-trivial task, I write down, even just in my head, what I think the answer might be. It's OK if it's a bad guess. You're always welcome to change your mind in light of new information. Once you've read a well-written response, though, it's hard to imagine any other possibility. If you have no guidance whatsoever, ask for what Thariq Shihipar calls a blind spot pass: give the model what you know and have it find your unknown unknowns.
Am I asking it to help me think or to offload thinking from me? Both are OK, as long as you know which one you're doing.
What would have to be true for this to be wrong? Then go find out. A model's self-assessment of confidence is much less valuable than an actual test you can perform, so give it one.
Have I heard the counter argument from a different angle? When I've taken a hard stance on something that's somewhat open-ended, I'll ask more than one model to argue the opposite side, then review the output and form my own opinion. This takes longer, but I end up knowing much more about the subject.
Would I bet on this in front of the person who has to maintain it? This applies to code and to anything else that you're delivering. I believe that this is the bar for answerability.
What am I no longer practicing? Maybe it's some of the routine debugging. I'm OK with letting some of that go, but I want it to be intentional.
Verification as a habit
I've been writing a lot about verification lately because I believe that the bottleneck has shifted from coding to being sure you're right. When you give an agent the means to verify what it's doing, whether that be by way of end-to-end tests, property tests, or by way of actual app interactions, it can make a change, run the verification test, read the output, and attempt again all before you've looked at anything. This is what Boris Cherny calls "give Claude a way to verify its work" and I believe that this is one of the most critical components of achieving great results. Rather than reading every line, you'll be building these loops and reviewing the evidence.
You can also surrender verification. "Is there evidence that supports my conclusion?" becomes "Did the check turn green?" Agents make it so cheap to create tests that you'll see a lot of green, and you could have a passing test that doesn't catch a broken feature. If the test is written with the same mistake as the feature, it'll pass. And a green check only conveys one property. It's too easy to imagine it covers everything.
When a check goes green, ask what it proved. Then ask what it didn't.
Define "verified" upfront, because post-facto, you'll rationalize any outcome. 
The finish line for agent work should be something tangible: a test passing, a screenshot, a log or trace. This ensures that the criteria for finishing the work is factual, and not up for interpretation (and surrender) based on something like "it looks like it's done." When you receive a finish notification from an agent, before you look at the summary, first review the code snippet of the command executed and its output.
Claude Code can also self-critique (via a subagent in a fresh context) its own work as a sanity check, and it's worth baking that into the loop so it runs every time, not just when you remember. I still ask at the end "Did I miss anything?" That sounds silly, but so often, when I finish some complex feature work using a frontier model, look at it, review it, and then ask, "Did I miss anything?" It will then come back with two or three more things. That's why I always ask.
None of this needs to be the norm, of course; knowing when to go deep is a skill. My favorite rule of thumb from our write-up on how the Claude Code team does code review is: "If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval."
This applies beyond code as well. If an agent has synthesized fifty customer calls for you, or a competitive analysis, check a couple of the source documents to make sure the summary is accurate. Check a number that your recommendation depends on to make sure it's being calculated correctly.
Agents have made verification cheap to set up. What's difficult for you is knowing what good verification looks like.
Actually paying attention to what's generated
Say an agent gives you a 600-line PR. You roughly look at the structure. You don't read every line. The variable names look reasonable and the tests pass, so you approve it. But somewhere in the middle there's a subtle ordering change in a transaction boundary, or a flipped default on an edge case you never thought about. You did review it, I guess, but only for what you already knew you'd find.
Writing code and reviewing it are different skills, and there's a point where reviewing turns into rubber stamping. So read the diff as if the AI didn't write it, and then look past the diff at what the agent decided. Over a long session it makes a lot of small decisions for you: the defaults, what's out of scope, which requirement it reinterprets when two of them clash.
You won't see any of that in a summary that says everything went well, so ask it to list the decisions and assumptions it made. Then quiz yourself. Pick a few lines at random and ask, what about this line? What about that one? For a document, close it and try to write out the main argument from memory. Some have a habit I like for long sessions: have Claude write a report on the change, and then give you a quiz at the bottom, where the rule is "I only merge after I pass the quiz perfectly."
Understand what you're shipping well enough to defend it. Because at some point, someone could ask.
Agents can also guard your attention. For example, I have an open source project that receives a lot of pull requests. I'll use agents to help determine what's incoming, what's contrary to our guidelines, and where my attention is likely required. I rarely let the agents self-determine this, but they can narrow it down to where I should focus my attention, and then I can actually think about whether these changes are solving the right problem in the right way.
Then there's volume, and you have to be honest with yourself about it. I've called this the orchestration tax. It's the gap between what your agents generate and what you'd feel comfortable putting your name on. If finished work is piling up faster than you can get through it, another session won't help until you've fixed that: tighten the checks so less of it needs you, or slow down.
When you're producing more than you can stand behind, you're no longer reviewing. You're hoping.
Quality in, quality out
The human mental model is still involved, but instead of in the middle, it's at the front and end. You're putting your energy into the front-end of the task description and context, as well as the back-end of reviewing the output. This is why good input is so important to the quality of output, and I view good prompting as a critical thinking skill.
Historically, if you made a non-specific request, someone would challenge it, and you might realize, "Oh wait, I actually didn't figure this out." An agent often won't stop you there. It fills in what you left out and hands back something that looks done, even though the idea behind it is still fuzzy. I've written about this as intent debt, the implicit goals, constraints and rationale that may exist in artifacts you didn't write. Unlike other kinds of debt, nobody else can fix this one for you. The intent has to come from you.
Your prompt is a reflection of your understanding of the problem, and if you can't express it clearly, it may not be clear in your own mind.
Write your own request brief in your own words before you ask for help. Describe the audience, out-of-scope items, and the definition of done. When your second round of corrections hasn't got you there, stop tweaking and rewrite your prompt.
You can have the agent help you with this too. I like the distinction Andy Clark makes between delegating to an AI system and collaborating with it. In the latter case, you're in a virtuous cycle of mutual amplification: your prompts sharpen your output, sharpen your next prompt and sharpen your mental model of the problem. If it's not clear, ask the agent to interview you about what it doesn't understand. If you close the session having refined your own mental model, that's a sign of success.
Also be careful about the input. It's easy for each agent to just pass the previous agent's summary into its context, and before long the third agent hasn't read the original document.
You also need your own standards for output. I've played around with AI in lots of different creative mediums, and most of it never gets shown because it doesn't meet my standards. Things are all coming out nicely formatted and confident, so polish is no longer a useful signal.
AI may have made it faster to produce, but if I wouldn't feel comfortable attributing the output to myself, I won't output it.
When something doesn't meet your standards, note why in shared config, a hook or a test so that it doesn't happen again. That's how taste compounds, and noting why something didn't make the cut is good practice on its own.
"But the models will be better at this than me"
If you're as bullish on the future of this space as many people around me are, you've probably had this thought for a couple of sections. In a year or two, the model will be able to detect what I'd be able to detect, so why bother maintaining the skill?
You may be right on a lot of that detection, and I've been arguing for increasingly pushing detection to agents myself. But here's why I think it still matters: at the end of the day, someone is responsible for what ships. Regardless of how much AI helped, a human has to take responsibility.
The question of how much to trust an agent for any given task is itself a judgment call. Part of staying calibrated is reviewing the work, because what the models get wrong keeps changing. Anthropic's own research on its engineers and researchers calls out the trap as the paradox of supervision: "supervising Claude requires the very coding skills that may atrophy from AI overuse."
These are some of the things that matter most to me and that a better model won't solve: what are you building, why is it worth it, who does it impact and what are you willing to sacrifice? Those are all questions you need to answer. An agent can be helpful in working them through, and I would like it to be, but ultimately they're still yours.
You may offload the work and much of the auditing, but not the accountability.
Practices for the everyday
You don't need to do all this rigorously. Just plug in what works for your workflow.
Once a week, write a bit of code without an agent, or do one real thing that would suck if you forgot how to do it. (I've called this a calibration exercise, but I don't mean it as a moral one.) Once a month, write down what you've stopped doing and decide which of those you're okay not doing. One question from an old blog post of mine remains as valid as ever: How lost would you be if AI didn't exist?
If something is above your comprehension, go learn it. If I'm writing and I run into a phrase I haven't seen before, I could Google a one-line explanation and include it. I prefer to do a little research to properly understand it, so I can see where it fits.
Checking the machine properly is real work, and pretending otherwise is how teams end up not doing it. It isn't free, so schedule it as a line item and you'll actually get it done.
Skills that you stop exercising are going to go away, and probably faster than you might guess. Keep doing the ones you're not willing to let go.
What to bring with you
Be intentional. An agent can quiz you, interview you and show you its evidence, but only if you set that up. So set it up.
Be honest about your place on the spectrum. If you can't explain the answer, even with an agent's help, you've surrendered it.
Have a hypothesis. Formulate one before asking, even if it's bad.
A green check means one thing. What did it check? What did it not check?
Look for evidence. Read what it ran and what it returned before reading the summary.
Read to know what decisions it made. What did it decide for you?
Craft your prompt. How you write what you prompt shows how much you understood the problem.
Set a bar, and stick to it. If you wouldn't put your name on it, it doesn't go out.
Keep yourself in the game by manually applying the skills that matter. One thing you could do: Before you ask, write down what you think will happen, and after the agent is done, write down one thing it didn't check. Let me know if that changes the way you read the output. Think independently. Ask better questions. Take responsibility for the outcome.

The human mental model is still involved, but instead of in the middle, it's at the front and end. You're putting your energy into the front-end of the task description and context, as well as the back-end of reviewing the output. This is why good input is so important to the quality of output, and I view good prompting as a critical thinking skill.
Historically, if you made a non-specific request, someone would challenge it, and you might realize, "Oh wait, I actually didn't figure this out." An agent often won't stop you there. It fills in what you left out and hands back something that looks done, even though the idea behind it is still fuzzy. I've written about this as intent debt, the implicit goals, constraints and rationale that may exist in artifacts you didn't write. Unlike other kinds of debt, nobody else can fix this one for you. The intent has to come from you.
Your prompt is a reflection of your understanding of the problem, and if you can't express it clearly, it may not be clear in your own mind.
Write your own request brief in your own words before you ask for help. Describe the audience, out-of-scope items, and the definition of done. When your second round of corrections hasn't got you there, stop tweaking and rewrite your prompt.
You can have the agent help you with this too. I like the distinction Andy Clark makes between delegating to an AI system and collaborating with it. In the latter case, you're in a virtuous cycle of mutual amplification: your prompts sharpen your output, sharpen your next prompt and sharpen your mental model of the problem. If it's not clear, ask the agent to interview you about what it doesn't understand. If you close the session having refined your own mental model, that's a sign of success.
Also be careful about the input. It's easy for each agent to just pass the previous agent's summary into its context, and before long the third agent hasn't read the original document.
You also need your own standards for output. I've played around with AI in lots of different creative mediums, and most of it never gets shown because it doesn't meet my standards. Things are all coming out nicely formatted and confident, so polish is no longer a useful signal.
AI may have made it faster to produce, but if I wouldn't feel comfortable attributing the output to myself, I won't output it.
When something doesn't meet your standards, note why in shared config, a hook or a test so that it doesn't happen again. That's how taste compounds, and noting why something didn't make the cut is good practice on its own.
"But the models will be better at this than me"
If you're as bullish on the future of this space as many people around me are, you've probably had this thought for a couple of sections. In a year or two, the model will be able to detect what I'd be able to detect, so why bother maintaining the skill?
You may be right on a lot of that detection, and I've been arguing for increasingly pushing detection to agents myself. But here's why I think it still matters: at the end of the day, someone is responsible for what ships. Regardless of how much AI helped, a human has to take responsibility.
The question of how much to trust an agent for any given task is itself a judgment call. Part of staying calibrated is reviewing the work, because what the models get wrong keeps changing. Anthropic's own research on its engineers and researchers calls out the trap as the paradox of supervision: "supervising Claude requires the very coding skills that may atrophy from AI overuse."
These are some of the things that matter most to me and that a better model won't solve: what are you building, why is it worth it, who does it impact and what are you willing to sacrifice? Those are all questions you need to answer. An agent can be helpful in working them through, and I would like it to be, but ultimately they're still yours.
You may offload the work and much of the auditing, but not the accountability.
Practices for the everyday
You don't need to do all this rigorously. Just plug in what works for your workflow.
Once a week, write a bit of code without an agent, or do one real thing that would suck if you forgot how to do it. (I've called this a calibration exercise, but I don't mean it as a moral one.) Once a month, write down what you've stopped doing and decide which of those you're okay not doing. One question from an old blog post of mine remains as valid as ever: How lost would you be if AI didn't exist?
If something is above your comprehension, go learn it. If I'm writing and I run into a phrase I haven't seen before, I could Google a one-line explanation and include it. I prefer to do a little research to properly understand it, so I can see where it fits.
Checking the machine properly is real work, and pretending otherwise is how teams end up not doing it. It isn't free, so schedule it as a line item and you'll actually get it done.
Skills that you stop exercising are going to go away, and probably faster than you might guess. Keep doing the ones you're not willing to let go.
What to bring with you
Be intentional. An agent can quiz you, interview you and show you its evidence, but only if you set that up. So set it up.
Be honest about your place on the spectrum. If you can't explain the answer, even with an agent's help, you've surrendered it.
Have a hypothesis. Formulate one before asking, even if it's bad.
A green check means one thing. What did it check? What did it not check?
Look for evidence. Read what it ran and what it returned before reading the summary.
Read to know what decisions it made. What did it decide for you?
Craft your prompt. How you write what you prompt shows how much you understood the problem.
Set a bar, and stick to it. If you wouldn't put your name on it, it doesn't go out.
Keep yourself in the game by manually applying the skills that matter. One thing you could do: Before you ask, write down what you think will happen, and after the agent is done, write down one thing it didn't check. Let me know if that changes the way you read the output. Think independently. Ask better questions. Take responsibility for the outcome.

content.text:
## 진행 결과

1. **소개 페이지에서 CLI 문구를 뺐어요.** 고친 파일은 5개예요. `index.html`, `index_n.html`, `about`, `guide`, `brochure`. 다시 검색해 보니 CLI라는 말은 하나도 남지 않았어요. 아티팩트는 Version 2로 다시 게시했어요. 링크는 같아요: https://claude.ai/artifact/2aTFkboGqWbTfc7SPANkXP
2. **캐시 폴더는 아직 지우지 못했어요.** 자동 모드 권한 검사가 삭제를 막았어요. 지금 쓰이지 않는 폴더라서 바로 문제가 되지는 않아요. 직접 지우려면 아래 명령을 입력해 주세요.
   `! rm -rf ~/.claude/plugins/cache/sc4sap/sc4sap/0.6.53`
3. **`package.json` 정리는 끝났어요.** 없는 파일을 가리키던 `bin` 줄을 `package.json`과 `package-lock.json`에서 지웠어요. 두 파일 모두 JSON으로 정상적으로 읽히는지 확인했어요. 커밋은 하지 않았어요. 지금 브랜치가 `enterprise`라서, 공개판에도 반영할지 정해야 해요.

## 글의 방식을 sc4sap에 적용하는 것에 대한 의견

적용하는 데 찬성해요. sc4sap 결과물은 실제 SAP 변경, 명세서, 고객에게 넘기는 문서로 이어져요. 글에서 말하는 "틀리면 다른 사람이 감당하는 일"에 해당해요. 그런데 sc4sap은 이미 일부를 하고 있어요. analyze-code의 Haiku 근거 확인, sap-critic, 사용자가 tcode에서 직접 확인하는 규칙이 그 예예요. 그래서 새로 만들기보다 빈 곳을 메우는 쪽이 맞다고 봐요.

**효과가 클 것 (먼저 적용 추천)**

1. **"결정과 가정" 섹션을 필수로.** create-program, program-to-spec, config-to-document 같은 결과물 끝에 에이전트가 대신 정한 것을 적어요.
   - 고른 기본값
   - 범위에서 뺀 것
   - 요구사항이 서로 부딪칠 때 어떻게 해석했는지

   글에서 요약에는 안 보인다고 한 바로 그 부분이에요.
2. **"검증 완료"를 미리 정하기.** 스킬마다 끝났다는 기준을 사실로 적어 둬요. 예를 들어 create-program이라면 아래 항목이에요.
   - 활성화 결과
   - `GetInactiveObjects`가 비어 있음
   - RunUnitTest 실제 출력

   보고할 때는 실행한 도구 호출과 그 출력을 요약보다 먼저 보여 줘요.
3. **"이 체크가 증명하지 않는 것"을 같이 쓰기.** 통과한 체크 옆에 한 줄씩 붙여요. 예를 들면 "활성화 성공 ≠ 업무 로직이 맞음"이에요. SmartForms 작업 때 "SSF_CHECK 통과 ≠ Form Painter 정상"을 겪었잖아요. 그게 이 원칙의 실제 사례예요.

**선택 사항으로 둘 것**

4. **원본 표본 대조.** module-to-process나 config-to-document처럼 여러 자료를 합치는 스킬에서, 주장 몇 개를 무작위로 골라 소스 줄이나 테이블 값과 다시 맞춰 봐요. analyze-code에 있는 근거 확인 방식을 넓히는 거예요.
5. **가설 먼저 받기.** analyze-symptom을 시작할 때 "예상하는 원인이 있나요?"를 선택 질문으로 넣어요.
6. **새 컨텍스트 비평가 기본 적용.** PRD 등급 연결, 트랜스포트 반입 같은 위험한 경우에만 기본으로 켜요.

**조심할 것**

- **비용.** 단계가 늘면 eco 모드의 의미가 줄어요. 1~3은 출력 형식만 바꾸는 거라 비용이 거의 안 들어요. 4와 6은 standard 모드에서만 돌리는 게 맞아요.
- **사용자 피로.** 글에 나온 퀴즈를 통과해야 머지하는 방식은 개발자 개인 습관으로는 좋아요. 하지만 컨설턴트가 쓰는 도구에서 강제하면 번거롭기만 해요. 넣더라도 opt-in이어야 해요.
- **구조.** 스킬마다 따로 쓰면 MD 200줄 제한에 걸려요. 공통 규칙 파일(예: `common/verification-evidence.md`) 하나를 두고 스킬이 참조하게 하는 게 나아요.

**추천 순서:** 1~3을 공통 규칙으로 만들어요. 그다음 create-program과 analyze-symptom 두 스킬에 먼저 시험 적용하고, 결과물이 어떻게 달라지는지 보고 넓혀요.

진행할까요? 그 전에 하나 정해 주세요. 공개판(`active`)에 넣을지, enterprise에만 넣을지예요.

---
name: analyze-symptom
description: Read-only, step-by-step root cause analysis for SAP operational errors. Reads the dump summary and failing source via MCP (known-issue web lookup only when the failure is in standard SAP code), widens to transports and where-used only when the clues call for it, narrows hypotheses with minimal user questions, and provides SAP Note search keywords. # SC4SAP Analyze Symptom

Performs structured root cause analysis for SAP operational incidents by connecting to the live SAP system through MCP. Auto-collects evidence from dumps, system state, recent transports, and code call graphs before asking the user any question.


<Purpose>
sc4sap:analyze-symptom is the first-line triage skill for SAP production incidents. Rather than bombarding the user with questions, it **directly investigates the SAP system through MCP** to gather evidence it can collect on its own. It then asks the user only about gaps that MCP cannot fill, narrows hypotheses to 2–3 categories, and produces SAP Note search keywords plus recommended next actions.
</Purpose>

<Response_Prefix>
Every response triggered by this skill MUST begin with `[Model: <main-model> · Dispatched: <sub-summary>]` per [`../../common/model-routing-rule.md`](../../common/model-routing-rule.md) § Response Prefix Convention.
</Response_Prefix>
<Target_Object>The target object is looked up on the active profile's system only. Not found → stop and ask per [`../../common/multi-profile-artifact-resolution.md`](../../common/multi-profile-artifact-resolution.md) § Target object not on the active system — never substitute a similar name, never switch profiles on your own.</Target_Object>

<Phase_Banner>
Multi-phase skill. Before each `Agent(...)` dispatch, emit `▶ phase=<id> (<label>) · agent=<name> · model=<Opus|Sonnet|Haiku>` per [`../../common/model-routing-rule.md`](../../common/model-routing-rule.md) § Phase Banner Convention. Resolve the dispatch mode first per [`../../common/model-dispatch-mode.md`](../../common/model-dispatch-mode.md): `auto` (default) uses the model below/in the rule; `user-defined` asks the user Opus / Sonnet / Haiku (recommended one first) before each dispatch group.
</Phase_Banner>

<Use_When>
- User reports a symptom using words like "error", "dump", "failing", "broken", "not working", "timeout", "slow"
- User has at least one clue: error message, TCode, program name, job name, or affected user/data
- User is unsure which log or transaction to inspect (ST22, SM21, SLG1, SU53, SM13, SM58, WE02, etc.)
- Need to classify whether the issue is custom development vs SAP standard
- Need to trace root cause of an incident that started after a recent transport or patch
</Use_When>

<Do_Not_Use_When>
- Root cause is already identified and only a code fix is needed — use `/sc4sap:create-program` or direct MCP `Update*` calls
- Pure static code quality review — use `/sc4sap:analyze-code`
- Need to create a new ABAP object — use `/sc4sap:create-object`
- Conceptual or configuration-guide question — use a module consultant agent directly
</Do_Not_Use_When>

<Session_Trust_Bootstrap>
**MANDATORY — runs as Step 0 before any MCP call or user interaction.**

Invoke `/sc4sap:trust-session` with `parent_skill=sc4sap:analyze-symptom` to pre-grant all MCP tool + file-op permissions for this session (eliminates per-tool "Allow this tool?" prompts during auto-investigation — `RuntimeAnalyzeDump`, `ListTransports`, `GetWhereUsed`, etc.).

- Headless host (system prompt declares `Host: sc4sap-web`) → skip entirely; the host governs permissions.
- If `.sc4sap/session-trust.log` already has a line within the last 24h, skip silently. Otherwise run it.

Full spec: see [`../trust-session/SKILL.md`](../trust-session/SKILL.md).
</Session_Trust_Bootstrap>

<Core_Principles>
- **Read-only, always**: analysis and reading only — no SAP write tools (Create/Update/Delete/Patch/Write/Activate, RunUnitTest, RuntimeRun*/RuntimeCreate*, CreateTransport), no Edit/Write, even when the user asks for the fix. Fixes appear only as proposals.
- **Cheapest evidence first**: dump metadata and termination link, then the one failing include; the ~50 KB formatted dump only when those cannot explain the error. A short web lookup (standard identifiers only — never Z*/Y* names, SID, user IDs, or data) runs only when the failure point is standard SAP code. Never re-ask what MCP can answer.
- **Evidence over assumption**: Do not speculate. No "probably" statements without supporting MCP or user-provided evidence.
- **Minimal questions**: At most 3 questions per round. Skip any question whose answer is already known via MCP.
- **Hypothesis narrowing**: Reduce candidate causes to 2–3 from the 8-category framework; each must carry a confidence level and a confirmation path.
- **Actionable output**: Every hypothesis must include the next evidence step (another MCP call, a TCode, or an escalation target).
- **Customization cache first (local, before live MCP) when a Z*/Y* object or customized SAP include appears in the trace**: read `<CUSTOMIZATION_DIR>/<MODULE>/{enhancements,extensions}.json` (the path Step 1 resolves once — never search for it) and correlate — a `Z*` class in a dump may be a known BAdI impl, a customized `MV45AFZZ`/`ZXRSRU01` may be a recorded form-based exit, a failing field may be a recorded append. Follow `common/customization-lookup.md`. If the cache is absent, suggest `/sc4sap:setup customizations` but do not block the current analysis.
</Core_Principles>

<Analysis_Framework>
All hypotheses must map to one of these 8 root cause categories:

| Category | Typical Symptoms | Key Signals |
|----------|------------------|-------------|
| Master / Input data | Only specific data fails, others succeed | Data values, related master records |
| Authorization | Only specific users fail | SU53, STAUTHTRACE, recent role changes |
| Customizing | Only specific org units affected | SPRO values, recent customizing transports |
| Interface / RFC / Batch | External integration fails | SM58, SMQ1/2, SM37, WE02, BD87 |
| Custom development | Z*/Y* objects in call stack | Recent Z* transports, GetWhereUsed |
| Standard SAP bug | Only standard objects in stack; right after SP upgrade | SAP Note search, kernel/SP level |
| Performance / Locks / DB | Timeouts, increased wait times | ST05, SAT, SM12, SQLM |
| Operational procedure | Step order or prerequisite violated | Month-end, dependency job status |

Every hypothesis presented to the user must declare its **category** explicitly.
</Analysis_Framework>

<Evidence_Collection_Matrix>
Evidence collection strategy — prefer MCP auto-query, fall back to manual TCode guidance:

| Symptom Type | MCP Auto-Query | Manual TCode |
|--------------|----------------|--------------|
| Short dump / runtime error — **first** | `RuntimeListFeeds` (`dumps`, time window) when no dump ID is known → `RuntimeGetDumpById` metadata (~7 KB, termination link) → failing include; formatted dump (~50 KB) only when needed | ST22 |
| Known issue — only when the failure point is standard SAP code | `WebSearch` / `WebFetch` (SAP Notes, KBAs, SAP Community) — standard identifiers only | SAP for Me |
| Performance / long runtime | `RuntimeListProfilerTraceFiles`, `RuntimeAnalyzeProfilerTrace` (existing traces only — never start a run) | ST05, SAT, SQLM |
| Suspect program/class logic | `GetInclude`/`GetProgram`/`GetClass`/`GetFunctionModule`, `GetAbapAST`, `GetAbapSemanticAnalysis`, `GetWhereUsed` | SE80, SE24, SE38 |
| Recent change tracking | `ListTransports`, `GetTransport`, `GetObjectInfo` (Author/Changed-by) | SE09, SE10, SE16 → E070 |
| **Z\*/Y\* object or customized SAP include in trace** | Local file read (path from Step 1, no search): `<CUSTOMIZATION_DIR>/<MODULE>/enhancements.json` (→ `badiImplementations[]`, `smodExits[]`, `formBasedExits[]`) and `<CUSTOMIZATION_DIR>/<MODULE>/extensions.json` (→ `appendStructures[]`) | n/a — local cache only |
| Enhancement / BAdI | `GetEnhancements`, `GetEnhancementImpl`, `GetEnhancementSpot` | SE18, SE19, SMOD, CMOD |
| System / session info | `GetSession` | /n (status), /o SM04 |
| Table schema (not rows) | `GetTable`, `GetStructure`, `GetView`, `GetDataElement`, `GetDomain` | SE11 |
| Unit test results | `GetUnitTestResult`, `RunUnitTest` | SE80 → test class |
| Authorization error | (MCP not supported) | SU53, STAUTHTRACE |
| Application log | (MCP not supported) | SLG1 |
| System log | (MCP not supported) | SM21 |
| Update error | (MCP not supported) | SM13 |
| RFC / tRFC / qRFC | (MCP not supported) | SM58, SMQ1, SMQ2 |
| Background job | (MCP not supported) | SM37 |
| IDoc | (MCP not supported) | WE02, WE05, BD87 |
| OData / Fiori | (MCP not supported) | /IWFND/ERROR_LOG, /IWBEP/ERROR_LOG |

**Rule**: For any MCP-supported item, never ask the user — query it directly.
</Evidence_Collection_Matrix>

<Workflow_Steps>
**MANDATORY**: Follow the step sequence defined in [`workflow-steps.md`](workflow-steps.md).

Per-step model allocation (the main thread follows the session model — `model: inherit`; heavy analysis is delegated):

| Step | Owner | Model | Role |
|------|-------|-------|------|
| 0 Trust | skill-to-skill | Sonnet | permission bootstrap — skipped on a headless host |
| 1 Initial Triage | main | **Sonnet** | clue parsing (a screenshot counts) + `GetSession` + MODE (`quick-dump` \| `full`, and `quick-dump` is the default — see `workflow-steps.md` § Step 1) + customization path |
| **2 Investigate + Narrow + Report** | **`sap-debugger`** — `model: "sonnet"` for `quick-dump`, `model: "opus"` for `full` | **Sonnet / Opus** | Read-only. `quick-dump`: dump summary → failing source; returns `BLOCKED — needs full` when the dump alone is not enough, and main re-dispatches the round as `full` on Opus. `full`: dump / scoped transports / code / enhancement / customization; web lookup only for standard-code failures. Writes the user-facing report per `output-format.md` (hypotheses, questions, Note keywords, next steps). One dispatch per round. |
| 3 Relay | main | **Sonnet** | output the report verbatim; wait for answers → repeat Step 2 |
| 4 Follow-up Routing | main | **Sonnet** | pointers only when the user asks for the fix (apply the proposal in SE38/ADT outside this skill, /sc4sap:analyze-code, module consultant) — never a write call |

sap-debugger's tool set already covers the dumps feed (`RuntimeListFeeds`), `RuntimeGetDumpById`, profiler, transport queries, code reads, enhancement lookup, and customization cache reads — see the agent's Investigation_Protocol for the full inventory. A `quick-dump` round is read-mostly work (dump → source → explanation), which `common/model-routing-rule.md` keeps on Sonnet (§ Tier 2 — the debugger still explains the dump, so it is not a pure Haiku fetch); `full` rounds need cross-file reasoning (dump × transport × source × customization) and stay on Opus. Ambiguity resolves to `quick-dump`, never to `full`: the cheap path escalates itself when it cannot finish, and the expensive one has no way back.
</Workflow_Steps>

<Question_Strategy>
**Rule**: max 3 questions per response. Never re-ask what MCP already answered.

Priority when information is missing:
1. Exact error text + message class/number — the strongest SAP Note search key
2. TCode / App / Program / Job where the error occurs
3. Reproduction conditions (always vs intermittent; user/data/org specificity)

Situation-specific follow-ups:
- **Authorization suspected**: Does another user succeed with the same input? Any SU53 capture?
- **Batch suspected**: Does manual execution also fail? Any recent variant change?
- **Interface suspected**: Does SM59 Connection Test succeed? What is the IDoc status code (51/52/53/64)?
- **Custom development suspected**: (First run `ListTransports` + `GetWhereUsed`, then) Does TR candidate X match the timing of the incident?
- **Standard bug suspected**: Release/SP auto-detected via `GetSession`. Does the same symptom reproduce on QAS/DEV?
- **Performance suspected**: How much slower than usual? Which resource saturates first — DB / CPU / memory?
</Question_Strategy>

<Output_Format>
Per-round report template and the final-round consolidated report structure live in [`output-format.md`](output-format.md). Follow it literally for both intermediate rounds and the final analysis.
</Output_Format>

<MCP_Tools_Used>
Main thread: `GetSession` only (Step 1). Everything else runs inside the `sap-debugger` dispatch, so dump payloads, source and transport lists never sit in the orchestrator context. The authoritative tool list and call limits live in the dispatch prompt in [`workflow-steps.md`](workflow-steps.md) § Step 2: dump (`RuntimeListFeeds` dumps feed, `RuntimeGetDumpById` metadata, formatted view only when needed), one failing include (`GetInclude` / `GetProgram` / `GetClass` / `GetFunctionModule`), scoped transports (`ListTransports`, `GetTransport`, `GetObjectInfo`), `GetWhereUsed`, enhancements, existing profiler traces, DDIC schema reads. Never `GetProgFullCode`, `GetTableContents`, `GetSqlQuery` or any write tool.
</MCP_Tools_Used>

<Common_Pitfalls_To_Avoid>
- ❌ Asking the user for information MCP can retrieve (system info, program source, recent transports)
- ❌ Firing 4+ questions at once
- ❌ Diagnosing a root cause without an error message in hand
- ❌ Skipping the dump lookup when a dump is suspected and speculating instead (`RuntimeListFeeds` dumps feed — `RuntimeListDumps` can return an empty list)
- ❌ Changing anything — code, data, transports, activation — from this skill, even on request
- ❌ Running the full investigation (transports, where-used) on a plain dump with no change-history signal
- ❌ Searching the filesystem for config/caches, or rewriting the debugger's report in the main thread
- ❌ Deflecting with "contact Basis / dev team" without a concrete checklist and evidence
- ❌ Claiming a standard SAP bug before attempting a SAP Note search
- ❌ Pulling the ~50 KB formatted dump before the metadata and failing include were checked, trusting the `summary` key facts of `RuntimeAnalyzeDump` / `RuntimeGetDumpById` (they pick the wrong chapter), or reading a whole program with `GetProgFullCode`
- ❌ Blaming recent changes without inspecting transport history via `ListTransports`
- ❌ Listing 4+ hypotheses (narrow to 2–3)
</Common_Pitfalls_To_Avoid>

Task: $ARGUMENTS
======
# Output Format — analyze-symptom

Report template for each analysis round of `/sc4sap:analyze-symptom`. Referenced from `SKILL.md`.

Written once, by the `sap-debugger` dispatch, in the user's language — the main thread relays it verbatim (see `workflow-steps.md` § Step 3). Omit sections that would be empty. A `quick-dump` round whose cause is confirmed goes straight to the Final Round structure; keep it proportionate to the problem.

## Per-Round Structure

Each analysis round follows this structure:

```
## 📊 Symptom Analysis — Round N

### 🌐 Known Issues (only when a web lookup ran — leads, not findings)
- [{title}]({url}) — {why it may apply / whether the system evidence below matches}

### ✅ Evidence Collected via MCP
- **System**: {SID} / {client} / {release} / {SP} / {user}
- **Findings**:
  - {Finding 1 — MCP tool used}
  - {Finding 2 — MCP tool used}
  - ...

### 🎯 Current Hypotheses (by confidence)
1. **[Category] {Hypothesis summary}** — Confidence: High / Medium / Low
   - Evidence: {MCP findings / user answers}
   - Confirmation: {next verification step}
2. **[Category] ...** — Confidence: ...
3. ...

### ❓ Questions for You (max 3)
1. {Question 1}
2. {Question 2}

### 🔍 SAP Note Search Keywords (priority-ordered)
- "{exact error message}"
- {message class} {message number}
- {program / class name}
- {component} {keyword}

### 👉 Next Steps
- ✅ Can do now: {additional MCP queries / local actions}
- ⏳ After your input: {what requires the user's answers}
- 🚨 Escalation candidates: {target} — reason: {why}
```

## Final Round

In the final round (no open questions), produce a consolidated report with final hypothesis, SAP Note strategy, and recommended action list. Structure:

```
## 🏁 Final Analysis — {symptom summary}

### Root Cause
- **Category**: {one of 8 framework categories}
- **Confirmed evidence**: {list}
- **Confidence**: High / Medium / Low

### SAP Note Search Strategy
- Known issues found: {web hits that the system evidence confirmed, with URL — "none matched", or omit when no lookup ran}
- Primary keywords: {ordered list}
- Recommended Notes portal queries: {2–3 concrete search strings}

### Proposed fix — not applied
{Only when the cause is in custom code: a minimal code block and where it goes. This skill never applies it.}

### Recommended Actions
1. {action 1 — owner, urgency}
2. {action 2}
3. ...

### Escalation (if any)
- Target: {Basis / Development / SAP Support / Functional}
- Reason: {why}
- Artifacts to attach: {dump ID, TR number, screenshot refs}
```

## Round Counter

Track round number in memory across the conversation. Do not persist to file — each `/sc4sap:analyze-symptom` invocation starts at Round 1.
